scores.reference_label: Recognizably Trap, with its own character
scores.headline: 1 defect to fix before mastering

mastering_blockers: True peak is 0.05 dBTP, 1.05 dB above the -1.0 dBTP every platform asks for; 4x oversampling already finds 1 inter-sample overs.

dimensions.label: Clipping & True Peak
dimensions.headline: True peak above the delivery ceiling

dimensions.label: Phase & Mono Compatibility
dimensions.headline: Mono-compatible: correlation +0.96 against a 0.45 floor for Trap, and summing to mono costs only -0.08 dB.

dimensions.label: Loudness
dimensions.headline: Sits under the Trap reference with no clean gain left

dimensions.label: Limiter Behavior
dimensions.headline: Barely limited: short-term PSR holds 9.1 dB, above Trap's 4.0 to 9.0 dB window, with 0 flat-topped runs and a distortion index of 0.000. Nothing is being crushed; how far under genre level that leaves the mix is reported under Dynamic Range.

dimensions.label: Dynamic Range
dimensions.headline: Crest factor is 10.1 dB and TT-DR 4.4, outside Trap's 5.5 to 10.0 dB window but by too little, or at too healthy a level, to be worth a finding.

dimensions.label: Compression
dimensions.headline: The transient survives the processing: 8.7 dB of crest in each 50 ms frame, above Trap's 3.5 to 8.5 dB window, with an estimated 3.1 dB of gain reduction.

dimensions.label: Frequency Balance
dimensions.headline: Upper bass sits light against the Trap reference

dimensions.label: Mud & Low-Mid Buildup
dimensions.headline: The low mids stay out of the way: 150-400 Hz sits -11.3 dB against 60-120 Hz, inside Trap's -17.0 to -7.5 dB window, with 0.1 dB of 300-600 Hz boxiness.

dimensions.label: Harshness & Sibilance
dimensions.headline: Bright percussive transients above the Trap reference

dimensions.label: Kick / 808 Relationship
dimensions.headline: Sub energy runs hot against the Trap reference (+1 more in this dimension)

dimensions.label: Vocal Balance
dimensions.headline: No lead to balance: this is a beat, so the topline is somebody else's and the space where it goes is the point. Nothing about a missing or tucked vocal is scored against this file.

dimensions.label: Transient Impact
dimensions.headline: Hits land softer than the Trap reference

dimensions.label: Mix Clarity
dimensions.headline: Elements stay separately audible: clarity scores 0.49 against a 0.45 floor for Trap, with 5.7% of the mix's audible loudness sitting under its own masking threshold against a 6.6% ceiling.

findings.title: True peak above the delivery ceiling
findings.detail: True peak reaches 0.05 dBTP, 0.95 dB above the -1.0 dBTP ceiling every major platform asks for (Amazon Music wants -2.0). Nothing is clipped in the file itself — sample peak is -0.23 dBFS — but MP3 and AAC reconstruct the waveform between the samples, and the decoder will clip what the file does not. 4x oversampling already finds 1 inter-sample overs that are not over at base rate.

findings.title: Hits land softer than the Trap reference
findings.detail: The hits land softer than the Trap reference: punch scores 0.33 against a 0.45 floor for Trap. Across 1016 detected onsets the average hit sits 4.4 dB above its own level 50 ms later, with a 12.4 ms 10-90% attack and a smearing index of 0.54. The weakest band is sub at 0.15. The ear reads the drop after a hit rather than the peak, so a small fall-off buys a smoother, more continuous feel and costs the sense that the drums arrived. Worst at 1:21.5, across 6 flagged spans.

evidence.label: Punch index
evidence.detail: Transient peak against the level 50 ms later.

clarification.question: Is this meant to feel smooth and rolling rather than hitting hard?
clarification.context: Punch scores 0.33 against a 0.45 floor for Trap, and the average hit sits only 4.4 dB above its own level 50 ms later. A deliberately soft, continuous feel and a transient that was flattened somewhere in the chain give the same reading.
clarification.if_intended: It stays in the report as a description of the feel of the record and stops counting against the score. Attack time and smearing stay in Details as the numbers to compare against if you ever want the hits back.
clarification.if_not: Then the impact is being lost on the way out. Look at the weakest band in the evidence — that is where it is going — then check the drum bus and the master for a slow-attack compressor or a limiter doing most of the work.

findings.title: Sits under the Trap reference with no clean gain left
findings.detail: This sits under the Trap reference and cannot gain up to it cleanly. Integrated loudness is -11.30 LUFS against a -9.5 to -6.0 LUFS window for Trap, and there is only -1.1 dB of clean gain left before -1.0 dBTP — turning it up as far as the peaks allow still lands at -12.35 LUFS, 2.85 LU short. Being quiet is free (every platform leaves quiet tracks alone); what this costs is the choice: reaching the window from here means limiting, so the gain staging in the mix is what decides how much of it you pay.

evidence.label: Integrated loudness
evidence.detail: Trap releases sit at -9.5 to -6.0 LUFS.

evidence.label: Clean gain available
evidence.detail: Level that can be added before hitting -1.0 dBTP, with no limiting.

evidence.label: Delta vs Spotify reference
evidence.detail: Spotify, YouTube and Tidal normalize to -14 LUFS.

clarification.question: Is this meant to sit quieter than a released record — a mix going out for mastering, or a deliberately quiet master?
clarification.context: Integrated loudness is -11.3 LUFS with only -1.1 dB of clean gain left before the true-peak ceiling, so turning it up as far as the peaks allow still lands short of where Trap sits. Headroom kept on purpose and gain staging that ran out give the same reading.
clarification.if_intended: It stays in the report as a description of the level and stops counting against the score. The remaining gap is then framed as work for mastering rather than as a shortfall in the mix, and the report stops asking you to close it.
clarification.if_not: Then it is the peaks stopping you, not the mix level. Find the two or three transients setting the ceiling — usually a kick or a snare — and control those individually. That buys more level than pushing the whole master into a limiter, and costs less.

findings.title: Sub energy runs hot against the Trap reference
findings.detail: Sub energy runs 2.5 dB above where Trap masters typically sit: energy under 60 Hz measures -1.6 dB relative to the whole band, against a -16.0 to -4.0 dB window, and the sub macro band reads 5.2 dB over its target curve. Weight down there buys the size and the physical push the genre is built on; it costs limiter headroom, and none of it reproduces on anything smaller than a full-range system, so it is level the small speakers never hear.

clarification.question: Is the bottom octave meant to be this big?
clarification.context: Energy under 60 Hz measures -1.6 dB against the rest of the band, above the -16 to -4 dB window Trap masters sit in. Deliberate weight and an 808 nobody filtered look identical here, and neither reproduces on a laptop speaker.
clarification.if_intended: It stays in the report as a description of the low end and stops counting against the score. Sub-25 Hz rumble is still reported separately, because that part is almost never the same decision and it costs limiter headroom for something no system will play.
clarification.if_not: Then there is more down there than you meant. Check below 30 Hz first — that is usually where it is and it is free to remove. If the weight sits in the 40-60 Hz range instead, it is the 808 or the kick, and it is costing headroom the master will want.

findings.title: Upper bass sits light against the Trap reference
findings.detail: The upper bass band (120-250 Hz) sits 3.7 dB below where the Trap reference puts it: the band measures 0.1 dB against a 3.8 dB target for Trap, which is 1.2 dB outside the +/-2.5 dB of room the reference leaves there, while low bass next to it sits -0.2 dB from its own target. Overall tilt is -4.5 dB/decade against -4.5 dB/decade for the Trap curve, so the overall slope matches and this is one band, not a tonality. That buys clarity and headroom and costs weight and size — worth keeping if it is the sound you want.

evidence.label: Upper Bass level
evidence.detail: 120-250 Hz, relative to the mix's own 1 kHz octave.

evidence.label: Spectral tilt
evidence.detail: Target tilt fitted from this genre's own curve over the same bands the measurement used.

clarification.question: Is the mix meant to sound this lean — 120-250 Hz, the body of the bass and the low end of guitars and piano?
clarification.context: The upper bass sits 3.7 dB below where the Trap reference puts it. This is a question about the tone of the record rather than about a number: a balance chosen at the desk and a balance inherited from the room, the monitors or a preset all measure the same from the file.
clarification.if_intended: It stays in the report as a description of the tone of the record and stops counting against the score. The band still appears on the balance chart against the reference, because the comparison is the useful part; it just stops being a fault.
clarification.if_not: Then the region is carrying less than you meant: the bass is probably all sub and no body, which vanishes the moment the track is played on a phone — a phone cannot reproduce the sub that is carrying it.

findings.title: Bright percussive transients above the Trap reference
findings.detail: The 5-9 kHz band is burstier than the Trap reference runs: it scores 0.673 on the burstiness index against a 0.64 ceiling (0.40 for Trap, widened because there is no lead vocal up front for the band to be protecting). The index reads how far the loudest frames in the band stand above the typical ones rather than how loud the band is, so a steady shimmer of cymbals and room does not register at all — but a consonant and a closed hi-hat are both short, bright noise bursts and the index cannot tell them apart. A beat has no topline recorded yet, so nothing up here can be a consonant. Without separated stems this is an inference rather than a measurement, which is what the confidence on this finding reflects — but a burst in this band is a burst whatever makes it, and percussion is the overwhelmingly likelier source. So this is the hats, shakers and rim clicks: transients landing hard in the same octave an 'ess' would, which means a de-esser is the wrong tool and a transient shaper on the percussion group is the right one. Hats cutting this hard is a choice, not a fault: it buys a top end that reads on a phone and through a rapper sitting on top of it, and it costs listening fatigue at volume plus headroom the topline is going to want.

evidence.label: 5-9 kHz burstiness index
evidence.detail: Attributed to the hats, shakers and rim clicks, inferred without stems — separate them to know for certain.

evidence.label: Voice-test confidence
evidence.detail: Below 0.65, or a lead sitting under the bed, means the 5-9 kHz bursts are attributed to percussion instead of consonants. Separate the stems to turn this inference into a measurement.

clarification.question: Are the hats and percussion meant to cut this hard up top?
clarification.context: The 5-9 kHz band is bursting at 0.67 against a 0.64 ceiling, and the bursts are percussion rather than consonants. A bright, cutting top is a genre signature in plenty of Trap; it is also what a stock sample and a bright bus produce with nobody deciding anything.
clarification.if_intended: It stays in the report as a description of the top end and stops counting against the score. No de-esser is prescribed — it is the wrong tool for percussion anyway. Fatigue at volume is still noted, because it is what the choice costs.
clarification.if_not: Then the top is getting away from the arrangement. A transient shaper on the percussion group, or a dynamic cut around 6-8 kHz keyed to the hats, keeps the brightness and removes the spit. A static shelf on the master takes the air off everything else to fix one source.

findings.title: Low end steps back in drop
findings.detail: The section this record is built to arrive at is the one carrying the least bottom end. Sub and low bass carry -5.9 dB of drop's own energy at 2:12.8 against -0.6 dB in drop at 0:58.1 — a 5.2 dB swing. It is measured as each section's *share* of its own level, so this is not the quiet parts being quiet: drop is within 9 LU of the loudest section and still has little under it. A Trap arrangement holds this to 3.0 dB across the 6 sections carrying the record. Taking the bottom out of the section everything else leads to buys contrast on the way in; it costs the moment the record exists for, and on a full-range system the drop reads smaller than the part before it.

evidence.label: Low-end swing across sections
evidence.detail: Sub+low-bass share of each section's own total, over the sections within 9 LU of the loudest. The ceiling is Trap's 3.0 dB scaled for a weakest section that is a payoff (drop).

evidence.label: Sections carrying the record
evidence.detail: 5 of them outside the intro and outro.

clarification.question: Is the bottom end meant to step back in the drop (2:13-2:38)?
clarification.context: Sub and low bass carry -5.9 dB of the drop's own energy at 2:12 against -0.6 dB in the drop at 0:58 — a 5.2 dB swing, measured as each section's share of its own level — so this is not the quiet parts being quiet: the drop sits within 9 LU of the loudest section and still has little underneath it. An arrangement that pulls the bottom out and a low end that went missing measure exactly the same.
clarification.if_intended: It stays in the report as a description of the arrangement and stops counting against the score. The swing stays on the timeline so you can still see where it happens, and no fix is prescribed for a section that is doing what it was written to do.
clarification.if_not: Then something is thinning the bottom there without being asked. The usual causes are a sidechain or bus compressor still keyed to an element that drops out in that section, a high-pass automated on the bass, or the sub simply not having been written in yet. Compare the section's sub level against the one either side of it before reaching for EQ.

findings.title: Narrower than the Trap reference
findings.detail: This sits 0.04 narrower than the Trap reference: Side/Mid measures 0.14 against the 0.18 to 0.45 window Trap works in. The widest band is presence at 0.43 and the narrowest sub at 0.00, with correlation at 0.96 and a -0.1 dB mono fold-down cost. A narrow field buys center weight and translates anywhere; this far in it costs the separation that gives each element somewhere to sit.

evidence.label: Stereo width
evidence.detail: Side/Mid RMS ratio. Trap sits at 0.18 to 0.45.

clarification.question: Is this meant to sit narrow and centered rather than spread across the field?
clarification.context: Side/Mid measures 0.14 against the 0.18 to 0.45 window Trap works in. A record placed deliberately tight and a record whose stereo content never made it out of the session look the same from here.
clarification.if_intended: It stays in the report as a description of the image and stops counting against the score. Mono compatibility keeps being reported, and it will read well — narrow is the safe direction, and that is worth stating rather than hiding.
clarification.if_not: Then the width is not reaching the master. Check for a mono-maker or a utility plugin left on the bus, and check whether the parts meant to be wide are actually panned or just double-tracked down the middle.

notes: The loudest section sits 1.7 LU above the median. That is a lift you can measure but barely hear; most records put 2-4 LU between the verse and the hook.
Loudest to quietest is 6.8 LU — drop at 0:58 (-9.9 LUFS) against intro at 0:00 (-16.7 LUFS).
The same part comes back at a different level: the drop at 0:58 is 2.5 LU louder than the one at 2:13. If that is not deliberate, it is a fader that moved between them.

Low end swings 7.4 dB across the sections carrying this record: sub and low bass are strongest in drop at 0:58 and weakest in intro at 0:00, measured against each section's own level. An intro carrying less underneath it is ordinary arrangement rather than a fault.
Stereo width moves from 0.08 in drop to 0.48 in intro — the image opens and closes with the arrangement.
